summary: This informational RFC presents real-world measurements, taken in August 2014 and June 2015, of how often packets with IPv6 Extension Headers get dropped in the Internet and where. The results serve as a problem statement for operational advice on filtering such packets.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7872 reports measurements of IPv6 packets with extension headers sent toward public servers. It found that some packets were dropped, including packets dropped by networks along the route.

subtitle: Measurements of IPv6 extension-header packet drops across Internet paths

tldr.problem: IPv6 packets with extension headers were suspected of being dropped, but measurements of how often and where this happened were limited.
tldr.mechanism: The authors probed public IPv6 web, mail, and name servers with Destination Options, Hop-by-Hop Options, and Fragment headers, then compared the responses and paths.
tldr.outcome: The measurements found drops for all three probe types and estimated that some drops occurred in transit networks. The results are from the measurement scenarios described in the RFC.

facts.label: Probe header size
facts.value: 8-byte Destination Options and Hop-by-Hop Options headers

facts.label: Fragment probe size
facts.value: Two fragments of about 512 bytes each

today: RFC 7872 is an Informational measurement report and the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its reported results describe the datasets and paths tested in the RFC.

sections.title: Why Measure IPv6 Extension Headers
sections.content:
IPv6 Extension Headers add functions to IPv6, including fragmentation. The RFC notes that packets using them had been suspected of being dropped, but that there was little concrete information about the extent of the problem.

RFC 7872 presents measurements made in August 2014 and June 2015. It reports drop rates for selected public server datasets and explains how other researchers can reproduce the measurements.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 extension headers provide protocol features, but network devices may drop packets that contain them. This RFC measures that behavior on selected Internet paths.

sections.title: Probe Method and Results
sections.content:
The authors gathered IPv6 addresses for web servers, mail servers, and name servers from the World IPv6 Launch dataset and Alexa's Top 1-Million Web Sites. They sent TCP probes with an 8-byte Destination Options header, an 8-byte Hop-by-Hop Options header, or a Fragment Header producing two fragments of about 512 bytes each.

In the World IPv6 Launch web-server dataset, the measured drop rates were 11.88% for Destination Options, 40.70% for Hop-by-Hop Options, and 30.51% for Fragment Header probes. In the Alexa dataset, Hop-by-Hop Options drop rates ranged from 39.03% for web servers to 54.12% for name servers. These percentages describe the probe results, not all IPv6 traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: The researchers sent three kinds of IPv6 probes to public servers. The measured drop rate depended on the header and the server dataset.

sections.title: Where the Packets Were Dropped
sections.content:
The study attempted to estimate whether a packet was dropped in the destination Autonomous System (AS) or in a transit AS. The authors report best-case and worst-case estimates because router-to-AS ownership can be ambiguous.

The measurements showed that some drops occurred in transit networks, outside the organization operating the destination. The RFC cannot determine whether a drop resulted from an intentional filtering policy, a device default, or a device fault. Its findings apply to the tested destinations and paths.
sections.plainLanguage: Some estimated drops happened before packets reached the destination network. The authors give ranges because they could not always identify which organization operated the dropping router.

sections.title: Troubleshooting Extension-Header Drops
sections.content:
The RFC describes comparing an IPv6 traceroute without extension headers with one that includes them. The ordinary trace shows a working path; the extension-header trace shows the last node that responds to those packets. Comparing the two may help identify the next node as the likely drop point.

This method has caveats: the two traces may not follow the same path, and the exact dropping node depends on where filtering occurs relative to the forwarding decision. The RFC identifies tools that can perform IPv6 extension-header tracing.
sections.plainLanguage: Compare a normal traceroute with one that includes extension headers. The difference can help locate a likely drop point, but it does not always identify the responsible device with certainty.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document presents measurement results and says it introduces no new security issues. It does not prescribe a filtering policy for packets with IPv6 Extension Headers.

The authors expect the measurements to support operational advice and repeated studies of how networks handle these packets over time.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC reports measurements and does not add a protocol or security mechanism. It is intended to inform later operational guidance.
